'''Anne Cooke''' ([[née]] '''Syme'''; born 14 November 1945) is a British [[biologist]] and academic, specialising in [[immunology]] and [[autoimmune diseases]]. From 2000 to 2013, she was [[Professor (highest academic rank)|Professor]] of Immunobiology at the [[University of Cambridge]]. She was a fellow of [[King's College, Cambridge]], between 1992 and 2013.

==Early life==
Cooke was born on 14 November 1945 in [[South Shields]], England, to William and Margaret Syme.<ref name="Who's Who 2015">{{cite web|title=COOKE, Prof. Anne|url=http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whoswho/U249453|website=Who's Who 2015|publisher=Oxford University Press|accessdate=14 November 2015|date=November 2015}}</ref> She studied [[biochemistry]] at the [[University of Glasgow]] and graduated with a [[Bachelor of Science]] (BSc) degree in 1967.<ref name="Who's Who 2015" /><ref name="bio - Cambridge Infectious Diseases">{{cite web|title=Professor Anne Cooke|url=http://www.infectiousdisease.cam.ac.uk/directory/ac416@cam.ac.uk|website=Cambridge Infectious Diseases|date=10 May 2011 |publisher=University of Cambridge|accessdate=14 November 2015}}</ref> She then undertook [[postgraduate research]] in biochemistry and [[immunology]] at the [[University of Sussex]].<ref name="bio - Cambridge Infectious Diseases" /><ref name="LinkedIn profile">{{cite web|title=Anne Cooke |url=https://uk.linkedin.com/in/annecooke |website=LinkedIn |accessdate=14 November 2015 }}{{dead link|date=July 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> She completed her [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (DPhil) degree in 1970.<ref name="Who's Who 2015" /> Her [[doctoral thesis]] was titled ''Characterisation of immunoglobulin synthesised by lymphoid tissue in vitro''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Characterisation of immunoglobulin synthesised by lymphoid tissue in vitro|url=http://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.452108|website=E-Thesis Online Service|publisher=The British Library}}</ref>

==Academic career==
Cooke began her academic career as a [[postdoctoral fellow]]. From 1970 to 1972, she held a [[Science Research Council|SRC]] postdoctoral fellowship in the Department of Biochemistry at the [[University of Sussex]]. From 1972 to 1973, she was a postdoctoral fellow at the [[University of Illinois at Chicago|University of Illinois]] and worked at the [[University of Chicago Medical Center|Medical Center]], [[Chicago]], USA. From 1973 to 1978, she held an [[Arthritis Research UK]] postdoctoral research fellowship in the Immunology Department of [[Middlesex Hospital]]. Then from 1978 to 1981, while remaining at Middlesex Hospital, she was a [[Wellcome Trust]] [[Research fellow|senior research fellow]].<ref name="Who's Who 2015" /><ref name="bio - Cambridge Infectious Diseases" />

In 1981, Cooke moved from research into teaching and research. From 1981 to 1988, she was a Wellcome Trust [[senior lecturer]] within the immunology division of the [[UCL Medical School]] and also at the [[Middlesex Hospital Medical School]].  During this time she collaborated with [[Joyce Baird (diabetologist)|Joyce Baird]], diabetologist at Edinburgh's [[Western General Hospital]]. <ref>{{Cite journal|last=Watts|first=Geoff|date=2014-11-15|title=Joyce Baird|journal=The Lancet|language=English|volume=384|issue=9956|pages=1742|doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(14)62064-X|issn=0140-6736|pmid=25473685|s2cid=10686320|doi-access=free}}{{Dead link|date=June 2022 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> From 1988 to 1990, she was [[Reader (academic rank)|Reader]] in Experimental Immunology at [[University College London]].<ref name="Who's Who 2015" /><ref name="bio - Cambridge Infectious Diseases" />

In 1990, Cooke moved to the [[University of Cambridge]]. From 1990 to 1996, she was a [[lecturer]] in the Department of [[Pathology]]. In 1992, she was elected a [[fellow]] of [[King's College, Cambridge]]. From 1996 to 2000, she was reader in immunology.<ref name="Who's Who 2015" /><ref name="bio - Cambridge Infectious Diseases" /> In 1999, she was a [[visiting professor]] at the [[University of Washington, Seattle]].<ref name="Who's Who 2015" /> On 1 October 2000, she was granted a [[Professor (highest academic rank)|personal chair]] and appointed professor of immunobiology.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Appointments|journal=Cambridge University Reporter|date=10 January 2001|volume=131|issue=13|page=9|url=http://www.admin.cam.ac.uk/reporter/2000-01/weekly/5832/9.html|accessdate=14 November 2015}}</ref> In 2013, she retired from full-time academia; she was appointed [[professor emeritus]] and made an emeritus fellow of King's College.<ref name="Who's Who 2015" /><ref>{{cite web|title=Emeritus Fellows|url=http://www.kings.cam.ac.uk/research/fellows/emeritus.html|website=King's College|publisher=University of Cambridge|accessdate=14 November 2015}}</ref>

==Personal life==
In 1969, the then Anne Syme married Jonathan Cooke. Together, they have two sons.<ref name="Who's Who 2015" />

==Honours==
In 2007, Cooke was elected a [[Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences]] (FMedSci).<ref name="bio - Academy of Medical Sciences">{{cite web|title=Professor Anne Cooke FMedSci|url=http://www.acmedsci.ac.uk/fellows/fellows-directory/ordinary-fellows/professor-anne-cooke/|website=Fellows directory|publisher=Academy of Medical Sciences|accessdate=14 November 2015}}</ref> On 18 November 2010, she was awarded an [[honorary doctorate]] by the [[University of Copenhagen]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Prof Anne Cooke awarded honorary doctorate by University of Copenhagen, Faculty of Life Sciences|url=http://www.path.cam.ac.uk/news/prof-anne-cooke-awarded-honorary-doctorate-by-university-of-copenhagen-faculty-of-life-sciences|website=Department of Pathology|publisher=University of Cambridge|accessdate=14 November 2015|date=12 December 2013}}</ref> In 2011, she was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Biology]] (FRSB).<ref name="Who's Who 2015" />
